amendments.why: ECC.10.20 renders בַּעַל כְּנָפַיִם as *that which hath wings*, where the English *hath* writes the lexeme of a noun rather than of a verb, preposition, suffix or הָיָה. Rule 46's closing paragraph already decides the unit — the supplied antecedent, the relative and the lexical verb all belong to the recast nominal, and a verb that is what the noun's own lexeme names is not rule 20's supplied lexical verb — but rule 43 is where a later pass will look for a *have*, and its added-clause enumerates only הָיָה, a possessive preposition, a suffix and a verb. Read on its own that sentence sends the ECC.10.20 *hath* to added, which would leave the one morpheme whose lexeme the word writes holding nothing, against rule 2. The amendment narrows the count to the morphemes of a clause the Hebrew wrote and points at rule 46 for a recast nominal; it adds no reading the contract did not already produce elsewhere, so nothing in the corpus can contradict it. Rule 43's own subtraction test is extended to name the noun case, and the rest of the rule — including the already-spent preposition and suffix limit, the relative-clause count, and the interrogative-particle limit — is returned unchanged.
amendments.rule: **Hebrew has no verb *to have*, so an English *have* is a recasting and belongs to whatever made the clause possessive.** Where `הָיָה` is present it is the existential and takes the *have* itself, its preposition goes `unrepresented` under rule 40, and the suffix takes the subject pronoun: `וַיְהִי לוֹ נָשִׁים` → *he had* … *wives* puts *had* on `הָיָה` and *he* on the suffix. Where the clause is verbless, the possessive preposition is what makes it possessive and carries the *have*: `לָהֶם מִסְגְּרוֹת` → *they had panels* puts *had* on `לְ` and *they* on the suffix, and `שָׁפְרָה עָלָי` → *I have a goodly heritage* puts *have* on `עַל` and *I* on the suffix. Where neither is present, a possessive suffix can be the possession by itself and takes the supplied verb with its pronoun: `טוֹבָתִי בַּל עָלֶיךָ` → *I have no good beyond thee* gives the suffix *I have*, headed on the pronoun. Another finite verb in the clause does not qualify merely by being finite. `שָׁפְרָה` is not a copula: the ASV renders it by the attributive *goodly*, which is its lexeme, so the *have* is not its. **But a verb the ASV has itself rendered by the *have* does qualify, and the same subtraction decides it.** Where the Hebrew writes a verb of falling or allotment and the English writes *have* in its place — `יִפְּלוּ בְנַחֲלָה` → *they shall have inheritance* — dropping the word leaves that verb with no rendering at all, so the *have* is the verb's own together with the subject pronoun rule 17 keeps there, and a preposition beside it whose relation the ASV has left unstated goes `unrepresented` under rule 40. **And where nothing in the clause makes it possessive, the word is not to be placed at all.** A clause that writes no `הָיָה`, no possessive preposition, no suffix and no verb the *have* renders has no morpheme to carry it: `יוֹסֵף חֲבָלִים` → *Joseph* ***shall have two*** *portions* leaves the supplied verb its own `added` unit under rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause, together with any numeral, subject or object the ASV supplies alongside it, while the possessed noun keeps only its own word. Do not fold such a word into that noun, into a neighbouring clause's verb, or into a preposition standing elsewhere in the verse to avoid the `added`, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and*: it is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them. **But that count runs over the morphemes of a clause the Hebrew wrote, and does not reach a *have* the ASV writes inside its recasting of a single nominal.** Where the Hebrew writes a noun of possession — `בַּעַל`, or another noun naming the owner or master of what follows — and the ASV recasts that noun together with its construct dependents as an English head noun and a relative clause of having, rule 46's closing paragraph governs: the supplied antecedent, the relative and the *have* all belong to that noun's own unit, because the *have* is what the noun's own lexeme names, and the unit heads on the *have* under rule 31, while the dependent keeps only its own English. `בַּעַל כְּנָפַיִם` → *that which* ***hath*** *wings* is one unit on `בַּעַל`, headed on *hath*, with *wings* left to `כָּנָף`. So ask whether what the ASV recast is a clause or a nominal before counting a *have* as unlicensed, and do not mark such a word `added` on the ground that the morpheme carrying it is not a verb. Test by subtraction, as in rule 16 — drop the *have* and ask which morpheme has lost its rendering. If only the possession relation is gone, the *have* is the preposition's or the suffix's; if a written verb, or a written noun of possession, is left with nothing, it is that morpheme's; and if nothing in the clause is diminished but a possession the English has supplied, it is `added`. **Read *no possessive preposition* and *no suffix* in that count as none the ASV has left an English word for.** A preposition or a suffix on which the ASV has already spent its own word stands in the same position as an absent one: it is not what makes the clause possessive, and it is not a home for a second English word, exactly as rule 52 counts a preposition's function words against the morphemes that could carry them and rule 51 says a waw holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one. What this rule's earlier sentences govern is a `בְּ` or a `לְ` that is itself the clause's predicate, for which the ASV writes no preposition at all — `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish* — and not a locative or other phrase the ASV has rendered in full. `אוֹ תְבַלֻּל בְּעֵינוֹ` → *or* ***that hath*** *a blemish in his eye* writes *in* for the `בְּ`, *his* for the suffix, *eye* for the noun and *a blemish* for `תְּבַלֻּל`, so nothing is left for the *hath* to complete and it is its own `added` unit; `מְרוֹחַ אָשֶׁךְ` → ***hath his*** *stones broken* goes the same way, the adjective keeping *broken* and the noun *stones*, with the supplied *his* `added` besides under rule 18's closing sentence. Count the clause's English words against the morphemes that could carry them before reaching for one that is already spent. **And where the possessive clause is a relative clause, count the ASV's words against the morphemes that could carry them before placing the English subject.** Where the ASV writes one word for the relative and the resumption together, that word is the relative's and it supplies the subject: `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish* gives *that* to `אֲשֶׁר` and *hath* to the `בְּ`, and the suffix is `unrepresented` under rule 22, since two morphemes point at the antecedent and the ASV writes one word for it. **But where the ASV writes a subject pronoun besides the relative, two English words answer to the two morphemes and neither is a surplus.** `כֹּל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ` → *all* ***that he hath*** gives *that* to `אֲשֶׁר`, *hath* to the possessive `לְ` and *he* to the suffix, which is the subject pronoun this rule's earlier sentences give it; the same clause written without a relative gives the suffix that pronoun in any case, as `מוּם בּוֹ` → *he hath a blemish* does. Count as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s, and do not mark the suffix `unrepresented` beside a written pronoun no other morpheme answers to, which would leave that pronoun `added` against rule 30 while the morpheme it realizes held nothing. A written `הָיָה` in such a clause still takes the *have* itself and leaves both the preposition and the suffix `unrepresented`: `אֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish*. **And an interrogative particle standing in such a clause does not take the *have* either.** Where `הֲ`, or the `אִם` opening a disjunctive question, stands in a possessive clause and the ASV marks the question by fronting the possessive verb itself, that word is the possessive morpheme's under this rule's earlier sentences and the particle is `unrepresented` under rule 17's sentence on a question marked by inversion alone: `וְאִם־זְרוֹעַ כָּאֵל לָךְ` → *Or* ***hast*** *thou an arm like God* gives *hast* to the `לְ` and *thou* to its suffix, and leaves the `אִם` nothing. Rule 20's fronted-copula sentence and rule 50's reading of an interrogative existential clause reach a copula the construction supplies and an existential frame, which are words no other morpheme licenses; a *have* is neither, since this rule assigns it to the `הָיָה`, the preposition, the suffix, the verb or the noun of possession that makes the clause possessive, and handing it to the particle would leave that morpheme holding nothing while the relation it alone carries went unrendered, against rule 2. Read what the fronted word is rather than that the clause is a question: where the ASV writes a separate question auxiliary besides the *have* — a *Do*, a *Shall* or a *Will* at the clause head — that word is the particle's under rule 17 as before, and the *have* still goes where this rule sends it.

conventions: Qoheleth's anarthrous substantival adjectives (חָכָם, כְּסִיל, סָכָל, עָשִׁיר) take the whole English noun phrase the ASV supplies to make them substantival, headed on the word carrying the lexeme (rules 31, 46): *the rich* at 10.6 and 10.20, *a fool* at 10.12. Where the ASV writes the construct chain as an English possessive, the supplied generic *man's* and the possessor's own determiner both join that adjective's unit and the construct noun (לֵב, פֶּה) keeps only its own word — *A wise man's heart* and *a fool's heart* (10.2), *a wise man's mouth* (10.12), the determiner going to the possessor under rule 29's possessive paragraph.

This chapter is heavily paratactic, and six of its seven added units are English connectives or subordinators standing over clauses with no conjunction morpheme in them: *so* and *and* (10.1), *that* (10.3), *which* (10.5), *and* (10.9), *yet* (10.14). Each was counted against its own clause's morphemes and left added rather than folded into a neighbouring waw, relative or verb. The seventh, *how* (10.15), is added because the לְ before לָלֶכֶת already holds the written *to*; do not read it as part of the infinitive's rendering, which rule 52's last sentence reaches only where no preposition stands.

Where a preposition, an interrogative or a construct noun stands with a following morpheme and the ASV writes one English word for the pair, the chapter fuses under rule 30 and heads on the morpheme carrying the content: כְּשֶׁ -> *when* (10.3), מַה־שֶּׁ -> *what* (10.14), מֵאַחֲרֵי -> *after* (10.14), מִלִּפְנֵי -> *from* (10.5), בְּ+suffix -> *therewith*, *thereby* (10.9), בְּלוֹא -> *before* headed on the negative (10.11), and the lexical pairs בַּעַל הַלָּשׁוֹן -> *charmer* (10.11) and חַדְרֵי מִשְׁכָּב -> *bedchamber* (10.20). In 10.11 the article segmented between the two fused nouns still takes the phrase's written *the*, exactly as rule 30 states for דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים -> *chronicles*.

The amendment narrows the count to the morphemes of a clause the Hebrew wrote and points at rule 46 for a recast nominal; it adds no reading the contract did not already produce elsewhere, so nothing in the corpus can contradict it. Rule 43's own subtraction test is extended to name the noun case, and the rest of the rule — including the already-spent preposition and suffix limit, the relative-clause count, and the interrogative-particle limit — is returned unchanged.

report: Cross-verse check: no split found. Every one of the 30 candidate lemmas differs only where the ASV's English differs. הַ (24 tokens) is aligned wherever a *the* is written and unrepresented wherever none is (10.6, 10.14, 10.17, 10.19), including the two places where another morpheme holds the phrase's one determiner — *every* on כֹּל at 10.3 s016, and the fronted anarthrous rendering at 10.15. וְ is read off the ASV throughout (and/but/then/also/yea), with both apodosis waws (10.10, 10.11) taking *then*. בְּ and לְ vary by written English only. שֶׁ fuses only where a second morpheme stands with it and one English word covers both (10.3 כְּשֶׁ -> *when*, 10.14 מַה־שֶּׁ -> *what*), and takes its own word bare elsewhere (10.5 *which*, 10.16 and 10.17 *when*).

Read the dump end to end for the split the table cannot see — a supplied word marked added in one verse and folded into a licensing morpheme in another. The chapter is consistent. Supplied *the* and *a* always join the nominal they determine (rule 15) and are never added; supplied copulas always join the predicate (rules 20, 49, and the gapped second line at 10.2); supplied substantival frames (*He that*, *whoso*, *the rich*) always join the participle or adjective (rule 46); and every connective or subordinator supplied beside a clause the Hebrew leaves asyndetic is added — *so* and *and* (10.1), *that* (10.3), *which* (10.5), *and* (10.9), *yet* (10.14) — with none folded into a neighbouring waw, relative or verb. The one non-connective added, *how* at 10.15, is right: the לְ already holds the written *to* and is not a home for a second word (rules 30, 52).

Two treatments that look opposed are both correct and say so in their notes: 10.6 שֵׁפֶל -> *a low place* heads on *low* (supplied generic noun) while 10.17 עֵת -> *due season* heads on *season* (supplied modifier). Rule 31's subtraction test runs in opposite directions there, so this is not a reconciliation candidate. Likewise 10.5's added *which* (a finite clause juxtaposed to a written antecedent, rule 55) against 10.20's *that which* joined to בַּעַל (a nominal recast as head noun plus relative, rule 46's closing paragraph) — the Hebrew, not the English, tells them apart.

BSB disagreements: none is a genuine error. The two מִן of 10.1 are the comparative left unrendered by the *outweigh* recasting, which is rule 35's own גָּדַל ... מִן -> *exceeded* example; the לְ of 10.14 is silenced by the bare indirect object *tell him* (rule 40); and the five Td are articles for which the ASV writes no *the* (rule 29). All three families are the documented convention difference, BSB attaching the morpheme to its phrase. No accepted edge was changed.

The in-verse correction at 10.10 (*do* to קִלְקַל, *not* to לֹא) is right and needs nothing further: rule 17's second limit gives a fronted *do* to the verb where no interrogative morpheme stands, and rule 35's closing sentence splits a negation and an auxiliary written as two words. The single large-source unit, 10.5 unit 12 (מִלִּפְנֵי -> *from*), is genuinely indivisible: one English word carries the whole relation and no morpheme owns a part of it (rules 23, 30).
Returned: no patches, three conventions for the log, and one amendment to rule 43 whose over-broad count would otherwise send a later pass to mark the *hath* of 10.20 added.
